summary: This Standards Track document defines the base syntax of Certificate Management over CMS, a certificate management protocol using the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is used together with the transport document (RFC 10003) and the compliance requirements (RFC 10004). It obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402.

eli5.summary: It is the paperwork format for asking for and getting digital ID cards.

questions: what is certificate management over cms
what is a simple pki request
subtitle: A certificate enrollment protocol built on CMS: how clients ask a CA for certificates and how the CA answers.

tldr.problem: Public key infrastructure needs a standard way for clients and registration authorities to request certificates from a CA, including for encryption-only keys that cannot sign a request.
tldr.mechanism: CMC wraps PKCS #10 or CRMF certification requests in CMS messages. A Simple request is a bare PKCS #10, and a Full request is a PKIData structure that carries controls such as identity proof, proof of possession, status and revocation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 10002 is the base syntax and obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402. CMC also needs the transport document (RFC 10003) and the compliance document (RFC 10004) for a full definition.

today: RFC 10002 is a Proposed Standard, was published in July 2026, and obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It must be read with RFC 10003 (transport) and RFC 10004 (compliance requirements).

sections.title: What CMC Is For
sections.content:
Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) is a certificate management protocol that uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). The RFC says it addresses two needs in the Internet PKI community: an interface to public key certification products and services based on CMS and PKCS #10, and a PKI enrollment protocol for encryption-only keys.

The protocol requirements in the RFC include building on CMS, PKCS #10 and CRMF where possible, supporting a plain PKCS #10 request followed by a "certs-only" response, doing all enrollment operations in a single round trip when possible, allowing all key generation on the client, including proof-of-possession methods, and supporting deferred or pending responses.

RFC 10002 is only the base syntax. CMC also requires the transport document (RFC 10003) and the compliance requirements document (RFC 10004). It obsoletes RFC 5272 and RFC 6402, merging the text of the second into the main document and folding in fixes from a list of errata reports. It also adds HMAC-SHA256 support, a direct proof-of-possession example for Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) certificates, and AuthEnvelopedData.
sections.eli5: CMC is a standard way to ask for a digital ID card, including for keys that can only lock things and not sign things. It reuses existing forms instead of inventing new ones.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Roles
sections.content:
Usually one round trip is enough: a PKI Request goes from the client to the server and a PKI Response comes back. Delayed issuance needs more. The RFC defines two request types and two response types.

  • Simple PKI Request: a bare PKCS #10 request, for when no other services are needed.
  • Full PKI Request: one or more PKCS #10, CRMF or other request structures wrapped in a CMS PKIData.
  • Simple PKI Response: a "certs-only" SignedData with no signer.
  • Full PKI Response: a PKIResponse wrapped in a SignedData or AuthenticatedData.

The roles are the End-Entity (EE) that owns the key pair, the Certification Authority (CA) that issues certificates, and optional Registration Authorities (RAs) that sit between them. A client is anything that creates a PKI Request and a server is anything that processes one, so an RA can be either. The protocol makes no assumption about transport, and the transports are defined elsewhere.

Renewal and rekey have no special services. They look like any other request, except that the proof of identity is an existing certificate from a trusted CA.
sections.eli5: You can send a short note asking for a card, or a full folder with extra papers. The answer is either just the card, or the card plus a letter explaining anything else.

sections.title: Full Requests: PKIData and Controls
sections.content:
A Full PKI Request is wrapped in SignedData or AuthenticatedData with content type id-cct-PKIData. The PKIData structure has four sequences: controlSequence (instructions called controls), reqSequence (certification requests in PKCS #10, CRMF or other formats), cmsSequence (nested CMS messages) and otherMsgSequence (arbitrary data referenced by controls).

Every element has a body part identifier, a 4-octet integer that must be unique within a single PKIData or PKIResponse. The value 0 refers to the current PKIData. A control is a TaggedAttribute made of a body part ID, an OID and values. The receiver processes controls in any order. The final server MUST fail the whole PKIData if a control is unrecognized and not marked processed, returning badRequest.

When a PKI Request is signed with a key from an embedded certification request, the request must contain a Subject Key Identifier extension and there MUST be only one SignerInfo. With AuthenticatedData, a shared secret is used through the Password Recipient Info option. A server must always answer a Full PKI Request.
sections.eli5: A full request is a folder with four trays: instructions, applications, attached envelopes and other papers. Every paper gets a number so the answer can point to exactly which paper it means.

sections.title: Proving Identity and Possession
sections.content:
CMC separates Proof-of-Identity (who the client is) from Proof-of-Possession (POP, that the client holds the private key). For identity, a client that supports Full PKI Requests MUST implement the shared-secret method. The shared secret is passed out of band. In Identity Proof Version 2, the client hashes the secret, then computes a MAC over the request sequence with that hash as the key. The result is the witness. Implementations MUST support tokens of at least 16 characters.

For signing keys, the signature on the request is the POP. For encryption-only keys, POP MUST be done by making the client decrypt a value, which takes more than one round trip. The server sends an Encrypted POP control with a challenge, the client decrypts it, and the client returns a Decrypted POP control derived from it. If it does not match, the server MUST NOT issue the certificate.

Because identity and POP travel separately, the protocol must link them so that one entity supplies both. The RFC describes three linkages: a witness derived from the shared secret (POP Link Witness), matching a subject name to the shared secret, and linking to an existing certificate. Clients and servers MUST support the witness and the existing-certificate techniques.
sections.eli5: To get an ID you must show who you are (a secret code the office gave you) and prove you really hold the key. For a key that can only lock, you have to unlock a puzzle the office sends you.

sections.title: Status, Pending Requests and Other Controls
sections.content:
Servers MUST use the Extended CMC Status Info control to report results. Its CMCStatus values are success (0), failed (2), pending (3), noSupport (4), confirmRequired (5), popRequired (6) and partial (7). A failed status carries a CMCFailInfo code such as badRequest or badIdentity.

If issuance is delayed, the server returns pending with a token and a suggested time. The client later sends a Query Pending control with that token. Clients MAY use a Transaction Identifier control, and Sender and Recipient Nonce controls give replay protection. A Data Return control lets a client have opaque state echoed back.

Other controls cover getting a certificate (Get Certificate) or a CRL (Get CRL), asking for revocation (Revocation Request), confirming a certificate was accepted (Confirm Certificate Acceptance), changing where a certificate is published, and batching several requests. The Get Certificate and Get CRL controls are optional to implement. The Publish Trust Anchors control lets a central authority distribute or update trust anchors as certificates.
sections.eli5: The office can say yes, no, or come back later with this ticket number. You can also ask for a lost card to be canceled, or ask the office to confirm you got your card.

sections.title: Registration Authorities and Encryption
sections.content:
An RA sits between the EE and the CA. To the EE it looks like the CA, and to the CA it looks like a client. An RA can batch requests, perform challenge-response POP, add extensions, archive private key material or route requests to different CAs. It can forward a request unchanged, add a new wrapping layer, or remove layers and add a new one. In every case an RA MUST NOT alter the certification requests themselves, because that would break the signature and the POP.

RAs have special controls. Modify Certification Request lets an RA replace or remove fields of a requested certificate. Control Processed marks controls the RA already handled. RA Identity Proof Witness says the identity check was done, so the CA never needs the secret. Response Body points to a nested response for the EE.

A Full PKI Request or Response may be encrypted by wrapping it in EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData. The RFC recommends adding a second signature outside the encryption layer. An RA that cannot decrypt a request MAY reject it unless it only forwards it. Section 9 also defines Extended Key Usage values for CMC CA (id-kp-cmcCA), RA and archive servers.
sections.eli5: An RA is like a local office that takes your application, checks it, and passes it on to head office. It may add notes, but must not change your signed application.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several risks. Replay attacks may need the nonce controls, and developers of state-constrained PKI clients are strongly encouraged to use them. Archiving a signing key needs extreme care, because the holder could forge signatures. Implementers should check cryptographic parameters, with the small subgroup attack named as an example.

Shared secrets should be generated with good random number techniques, since user-chosen secrets allow dictionary attacks. Anyone who has the shared secret can create a valid MAC, so SignedData should be preferred to AuthenticatedData whenever possible, and each message should be for a single entity.

Processing the Publish Trust Anchors control demands extreme care, because mistakes let an attacker change the client's trust anchors, which the RFC calls slamming. Upstream processors such as a CA MUST verify that an RA is identified and authorized to make the assertions it makes.
sections.eli5: The main danger is someone sneaking a fake rule into the system. So keep secrets secret, pick them randomly, and be very careful before trusting a new list of trusted offices.

messages.label: Full PKI Request
messages.note: Tells the server the public part of the new encryption key pair.

messages.label: Encrypted POP control
messages.note: A challenge encrypted with the presented public key.

messages.label: Decrypted POP control
messages.note: A keyed hash computed from the decrypted challenge.

items.label: success
items.desc: The request was granted or the action completed.

items.label: failed
items.desc: The request was not granted; more information is in the response.

items.label: pending
items.desc: Not yet processed; the requester polls back.

items.label: noSupport
items.desc: The requested operation is not supported.

items.label: confirmRequired
items.desc: A Confirm Certificate Acceptance control must be returned first.

items.label: popRequired
items.desc: A direct POP operation is required.

items.label: partial
items.desc: A partial response; the requester polls for the rest.
